title: Semantic Shift
paragraphs: Our forefathers advise us to rein in anger (ciṉam), as anger spoils relationships, destroys unity, and mars friendship. That is why anger is vicious. It should be avoided. Anger cannot be accepted in any form. But there are instances where the word ‘anger’ is used in a positive sense.
For example, when an army of brave youth rises to defend the Tamil language, we go in for expressions like the one below:
> Look at the upsurge of the angry tigers > That march up > Beating the drum of racial honour!
Though the emotion of anger is generally not accepted, the term attains a significant status in this context.
Pētaimai can be interpreted as ignorance. The dictionary defines pētai as a young woman. There are women who witness with glee the plight of a woman ‘possessed’ being thrashed by exorcists.
While denouncing such women as pētai, we are not using the term in any positive sense.

But if an old man who marries a young woman dies within six months of the wedding, we take pity on the young widow and call her a poor, unfortunate girl. When we use the word pētai for the young widow, the meaning changes. The word here does not denote folly but her pathetic condition as a young widow. Therefore in this context, pētaimai gains in stature as a special term referring to pathos.
When we call a person jealous or compare that person to Gandhari (Duriyodhana’s mother in Mahābhārata) we are using the term poṟāmai (envy, jealousy) in its derogatory sense.

But when the film Parācakti scripted by me became a roaring success, my good friend poet Kannadasan visited me. After hugging me, he exclaimed, “Sir, I feel really jealous of you.” He kissed me on the forehead. In this context the word parts with its negative sense to become something endearing and appreciative. Thus the word develops a special sense.
Poverty is not acceptable in any form. Eradicate poverty. This is the war-cry of progressive people and the vow of those in governance. Poverty no doubt is a cruel thing.

“I withered every time I chanced upon withered crops.” These are the words of Vaṭalūr Vaḷḷalār Rāmaliṅka Aṭikaḷār, a saint who had a great compassion for the poor and the downtrodden. As in the case of the two words discussed above, the word vaṟumai (poverty) too undergoes a kind of regeneration through Vaḷḷalār comparing it to withered crops.
Anger, ignorance, jealousy, and poverty are to be avoided by us. Be that as it may, there are contexts where they have a positive worth.
> The four traits of the hero and heroine-- > Anger, ignorance, envy and penury -- > Do occur in them > As attributes (implied) of their positive worth.
